title: Method and apparatus for automatically determining salient features for object classification

report.headline: Dead patent with a future (78/100, high confidence): the field is clearly alive, but the core technique appears commoditized, so any business would need to come from a specific vertical use.
report.what_it_is: A method for sorting documents by comparing a group you care about with a contrasting 'anti-content' group, then ranking the words or features that show up mostly in the first group. The top-ranked features are used to tell the two groups apart and classify documents.

why_it_died.text: Microsoft paid the 4th- and 8th-year maintenance fees and then skipped the third fee. The patent lapsed in 2017, about 5 years early. No reinstatement appears on record. The record does not say why the fee was skipped. The modest 'died for money, not merit' score (5.2/15) means the lapse alone does not show the idea was undervalued.

case_for.point: The field still looks technically active. The patent has 88 citing filings, 26 from unrelated owners after it lapsed, and 9 from 2019 on. This is why it scored full marks for 'field still alive' and 18/20 for momentum.
Examiners cited it against 13 later applications. That suggests it sits close to work people are still trying to patent today.
Specific companies, mainly the Autobrains/Cartica group, keep filing on top of it. They could be partners, customers, or a signal of where demand sits.

case_against.point: Very similar statistical feature ranking (chi-square, SelectKBest) appears to be freely available in scikit-learn and widely taught. The method alone is unlikely to be a moat.
The claims are long. The shortest independent claim is 224 words. Breadth at grant scored only 5.1/15, so the specific steps described may be narrow.
Citations show interest, not revenue. The market signals here measure patent activity, not paying customers.

blockers.point: Microsoft holds a later related patent that may still be in force: US9251473B2, 'Identifying salient items in documents.'
Five later patents by other owners were cited against this one and may still be in force.
Software classification is crowded with overlapping live patents from large incumbents. Data products may also face privacy rules such as HIPAA, GDPR and CCPA.
The patent describes the idea, not the working know-how. Expect to rebuild the practical details yourself, though open tools may cover much of it.

assumption_to_test.assumption: Buyers in one specific vertical (for example legal, compliance or support-ticket triage) will pay for a product that explains which features separate their 'relevant' documents from 'irrelevant' ones, rather than using free scikit-learn tools.
assumption_to_test.why_riskiest: The technique appears freely documented and widely taught. So all the value has to come from a vertical product people will pay for, not from the method itself.
assumption_to_test.how_to_test: Pick one vertical. Build a quick scikit-learn chi2 demo on public sample documents. Spend about $200 on a landing page and targeted ads offering 'see what makes your documents different.' Run 10-15 interviews with people who sort documents by hand. Success looks like at least 3 people agreeing to a paid pilot or a pre-order within two weeks.

attorney_questions: Do Microsoft's US9251473B2 or the five later patents cited against this one have live claims that could cover a document classifier built on contrast-group feature ranking?
Since the third maintenance fee was not paid and no reinstatement is on record, is there any remaining risk of revival or other rights tied to US6938025B1?
Are there recent Autobrains/Cartica or other incumbent filings in our target vertical that we should review before building?
report.disclaimer: Research and triage only, not legal advice. This report is not a patentability, validity or freedom-to-operate opinion. Patent status shown here comes from public records that can lag or be wrong. An expired patent is not the same as free to use: follow-on patents, regulatory exclusivity, trade secrets and standards can still block a product. Confirm with a registered patent attorney before acting.

signals.signal: Sustained technical interest after lapse: the patent continues to be cited by unrelated owners well after maintenance stopped, including a cluster of recent filings.
Recent citing activity is concentrated in one corporate group (Autobrains/Cartica AI), which suggests a narrow set of active builders rather than broad industry adoption.

The core idea, ranking features by statistical difference between classes, is now commodity practice in open-source tooling and teaching. Differentiation would likely need to come from application, data, or integration rather than the method itself.

The original owner stopped paying maintenance fees with about 5 years of term left and filed in only one jurisdiction. This hints the owner saw limited commercial value in keeping it, though the reason is not stated in the record.

read.who_is_active: Since 2019 the most frequent citing filer is Autobrains Technologies (7 filings across two name variants), alongside the related Cartica Ai Ltd and one filing from 深圳市斯维尔科技股份有限公司.
read.market_read: Citation activity shows the statistical salient-feature selection field is still technically alive, with recent filings led mainly by the Autobrains/Cartica group, but citations indicate interest, not revenue. Because comparable chi-square feature selection is freely documented in scikit-learn and widely taught, a founder should treat this as a crowded, commoditized technique and seek value in a specific vertical application; any freedom-to-operate question needs a patent attorney's review.

web.finding: scikit-learn's current documentation (v1.9.1) offers SelectKBest with a chi2 statistical test to keep the top-k features for classification, similar to ranking features by statistical difference between classes.
A tutorial on text-classification methods describes picking terms whose chi-square score shows they depend on the document's class, which suggests the approach is widely taught.
